title: NTA UGC NET English Full Mock Test #11
subtitle: 100 Questions · 200 Marks · Post-2018 NTA Pattern · Zero Answer Bias (25 A/B/C/D) · Reading Comprehension (Q91-100)

items.title: Mock #11 · Q1
items.stem:
Match the LIST-I with LIST-II
LIST-I (Genre) | LIST-II (Poem)
A. Dub Poetry | I. "Tintern Abbey"
B. Bucolic Poetry | II. Ariel
C. Confessional Poetry | III. The Dread Affair
D. Topographical Poetry | IV. "Eclogues"
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Dub poetry is represented by Linton Kwesi Johnson's The Dread Affair (A-III), bucolic (pastoral) poetry by Virgil's Eclogues (B-IV), confessional poetry by Sylvia Plath's Ariel (C-II), and topographical (loco-descriptive) poetry by William Wordsworth's 'Tintern Abbey' (D-I).

items.title: Mock #11 · Q2
items.stem: Which of the following definitions of various social variation in language is incorrect?
options: Convergence is a speech style that attempts to reduce social distance, and use forms that are similar to those used by the person we are talking to.
A register is a conventional way of using language that is appropriate in a specific context, which may be identified as situational, occupational or topical.
Jargons are words and phrases, often involving body parts, bodily functions and sexual acts, that people avoid for reasons related to religion, politeness and prohibited behavior.
Slang describes words or phrases that are used instead of more everyday terms among younger speakers and other groups with special interests.
items.explanation: In George Yule's The Study of Language, words and phrases avoided for reasons of religion, politeness, or prohibited behavior are defined as taboo terms, whereas jargon refers to specialized technical vocabulary used by a specific profession or group.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q3
items.stem:
Which of these books are written by Nirad C. Chaudhuri?
A. The Continent of Circe
B. Principal Upanishads
C. A Passage to England
D. Our New Rulers
E. The Autobiography of an Unknown Indian

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The Autobiography of an Unknown Indian (1951, E), A Passage to England (1959, C), and his Duff Cooper Prize-winning work The Continent of Circe (1965, A) are famous non-fictional prose works by Nirad C. Chaudhuri, whereas The Principal Upanishads (1953, B) was written by S. Radhakrishnan.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q4
items.stem:
Sexual possessiveness is a theme
of Shakespeare's
items.explanation: Sexual possessiveness, erotic jealousy, and patriarchal control over desire are central themes in William Shakespeare's comedy A Midsummer Night's Dream (c. 1595–1596), evident in Egeus's claim over Hermia, the tangled Athenian lovers, and Oberon and Titania's quarrel.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q5
items.stem:
Chronologically arrange the following texts in order of publication.
A. Betty Friedan’s The Feminine Mystique
B. Simone de Beauvoir’s The Second Sex
C. Virginia Woolf’s A Room of One’s Own
D. Germaine Greer’s The Female Eunuch
E. Adrienne Rich’s Of Woman Born
items.explanation: Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own was published in 1929 (C), Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex in 1949 (B), Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique in 1963 (A), Germaine Greer's The Female Eunuch in 1970 (D), and Adrienne Rich's Of Woman Born in 1976 (E). This forms the sequence C, B, A, D, E.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q6
items.stem:
In which of the following works does
Mrs. Malaprop appear ?
items.explanation: Mrs. Malaprop, Lydia Languish's guardian whose pretentious verbal blunders ('a nice derangement of epitaphs') gave English the word 'malapropism', is a famous comic character in Richard Brinsley Sheridan's play The Rivals (1775).

items.title: Mock #11 · Q7
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The theatre was at a greater popularity in Eighteenth century England.
Statement II: Theatre had court patronage in and around London.

In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
items.explanation: In eighteenth-century England, theatre expanded rapidly in popularity among a growing middle-class commercial audience (Statement I is true), whereas it relied on commercial ticket sales and the Licensing Act patent theatres rather than direct royal court patronage (Statement II is false).

items.title: Mock #11 · Q8
items.stem: Who proposed the idea that the mind at the time of birth is like a blank slate or tabula rasa?
items.explanation: In An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689/1690), English empiricist philosopher John Locke rejected innate ideas and argued that the human mind at birth is a 'white paper, void of all characters' (tabula rasa or blank slate) furnished entirely through sensory experience and reflection.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q9
items.stem:
Identify the correct pairs:
A. Kalidasa - Amoghavarsha
B. Bhavabhuti - Uttararamacharita
C. Bhasa - Urubhanga
D. Rajashekhara - Rajatarangini
E. Somadeva - Kathasaritsagara

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Bhavabhuti authored Uttararamacharita (B), Bhasa wrote the Sanskrit tragedy Urubhanga (C), and Somadeva compiled the eleventh-century story collection Kathasaritsagara (E), whereas Rajatarangini was written by Kalhana (not Rajashekhara).

items.title: Mock #11 · Q10
items.stem: What did Thomas Carlyle mean by "Close thy Byron; open thy Goethe" ?
options: Britain's pre-eminence as a global power will depend on mastery of foreign languages
Leave England and emigrate to Germany
Even a foreign author is better than a home-grown scoundrel
Abandon the introspection of the Romantics and turn to the higher moral purpose found in Goethe
items.explanation: In Book II, Chapter 9 ('The Everlasting Yea') of Sartor Resartus (1833–34), Thomas Carlyle's persona Diogenes Teufelsdröckh exhorts readers to 'Close thy Byron; open thy Goethe,' urging Victorians to abandon self-absorbed Romantic introspection and despair in favour of dutiful moral action.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q11
items.stem:
Match the LIST-I with LIST-II
LIST-I (Concept) | LIST-II (Meaning)
A. Aprastuta-Prasamsa | I. A statement conjunctively of the qualities and actions of things;
B. Vyajastuti | II. Where a similar good or bad consequence is exhibited by connecting a thing with another object
C. Nidarsanam | III. Where the praise of an object with which one is not concerned is made.
D. Sahokti | IV. Praise in the form of despair
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Sanskrit Alamkara Sastra, Aprastuta-Prasamsa is indirect praise of an non-contextual object (A-III), Vyajastuti is disguised praise in the form of blame or despair (B-IV), Nidarsana connects two things to exhibit a similar good or bad consequence (C-II), and Sahokti is a conjunctive statement of qualities and actions (D-I).

items.title: Mock #11 · Q12
items.stem: Which among the following is NOT an American Slave narrative?
options: The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Oloudah Equiano
Life and Adventure of Henry Bibb
items.explanation: Songs of Enchantment (1993) is a magical-realist novel by Nigerian writer Ben Okri (the sequel to The Famished Road), whereas the narratives of Olaudah Equiano (1789), Henry Bibb (1849), and Solomon Northup (Twelve Years a Slave, 1853) are historic slave narratives.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q13
items.meta: Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem:
Identify the correct options from the following statements:
A. Ecocriticism has often explained the ‘human and non-human webs of interrelation.”
B. In Ecocriticism, human accountability to the environment is part of the text’s ethical orientation.
C. Ecocriticism foregrounds the notion of an interplay between environment and the body.
D. There is only one wave of Ecocriticism.
E. Ecocriticism has not tackled the issue of gender.
items.explanation: Statements A, B, and C capture foundational principles of ecocriticism: the interconnectedness of human and non-human worlds, ecological accountability as a central ethical orientation, and the physical interplay between human bodies and natural environments. Statement D is false because ecocriticism has developed across multiple distinct waves, and statement E is false because ecofeminism is a foundational branch of ecocritical inquiry.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q14
items.stem: Who among the following is NOT a ‘University Wit’ ?
items.explanation: The 'University Wits' were late sixteenth-century Cambridge and Oxford-educated playwrights including Christopher Marlowe, Robert Greene, George Peele, Thomas Nashe, John Lyly, and Thomas Lodge. Ben Jonson was not university-educated and belongs to the Jacobean era.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q15
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of their publications :
(A) Love and Death
(B) Urvasie : A Poem
(C) Songs to Myrtilla
(D) Savitri
(E) Chitrangada
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Aurobindo's Songs to Myrtilla (1895) and Urvasie (1896) came first, then Tagore's Chitrangada, Love and Death and finally Aurobindo's epic Savitri. So the order is C, B, E, A, D.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q16
items.stem:
Which statement is not true of
Benedict
Anderson's
Imagined
Communities ?
options: Anderson's view, modern nationalism was basically a consequence of the convergence of capitalism, the new print technology and the fixity that resulted from print extending to 'Vernacular' languages
It is subtitled Reflections on the Origin and Spread of Nationalism
In this book, Anderson advances the view that nations are not natural entities but narrative constructs
It is a prosaic response to the myth of El Dorado
items.explanation: Benedict Anderson's Imagined Communities: Reflections on the Origin and Spread of Nationalism (1983) argues that nations are socially constructed 'imagined communities' shaped by print-capitalism and vernacular print languages. It is not a response to the myth of El Dorado.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q17
items.stem:
Given below are two statements : One is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R.
Assertion (A): English today is not only the language we teach but also the subject that enables its learners to become subtle and tough minded readers
Reason (R): Students are encouraged to think and analyse the historical and ontological status of the texts they read, and how best to read them.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct
items.explanation: Learners become subtle, tough-minded readers precisely because they are taught to analyse the status of texts, so R explains A.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q18
items.stem:
To hom does Francis Bacon offer the following piece of advice ?
“Let him sequester himself from the Company of his Countrymen, and diet in such Places,
here there is good company of the Nation... Let him upon his Removes, ... procure
Recommendation, to some person of Quality, residing in the Place, hither he removeth...”
items.explanation: In his essay 'Of Travel' (1625), Francis Bacon advises the young gentleman traveller to avoid cloistering with fellow countrymen, to eat where there is local company, and to carry letters of recommendation to persons of quality at every stop.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q19
items.stem:
Who among the following are writers of wordless graphic narratives?
A. Roy Fuller
B. Orijit Sen
C. Anthony Hecht
D. George Mathen Appupen
E. George Monbiot
items.explanation: Orijit Sen (creator of The River of Stories) and Appupen (pen name of George Mathen, author of wordless graphic narratives like Moonward and Legends of Halahala) are Indian graphic novel writers and artists, confirming B and D as the correct pair.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q20
items.stem:
In Jeremy Collier's 1698 pamphlet attacking the immorality and profaneness of the
English stage, who among the following was the principal target ?
items.explanation: In A Short View of the Immorality and Profaneness of the English Stage (1698), Jeremy Collier fiercely attacked contemporary Restoration comedy, singling out Sir John Vanbrugh (author of The Relapse and The Provok'd Wife) and William Congreve as principal targets.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q21
items.stem:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Autobiography)
A. My Second Innings
B. Justice for the Judge: An Autobiography
C. My Country My Life
D. Through the Broken Glass

List II (Writer)
I. T.N. Seshan
II. L.K. Advani
III. Ranjan Gogoi
IV. Shanti Bhushan

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A - IV, B - III, C - II, D - I
A - III, B - II, C - I, D - IV
A - I, B - IV, C - III, D - II
A - II, B - I, C - IV, D - III
items.explanation: Shanti Bhushan authored the legal memoir My Second Innings (A-IV); former Chief Justice of India Ranjan Gogoi wrote Justice for the Judge: An Autobiography (B-III); L.K. Advani penned My Country My Life (C-II); and former Chief Election Commissioner T.N. Seshan wrote Through the Broken Glass (D-I).

items.title: Mock #11 · Q22
items.stem: Which among the following texts can be characterised as a lesbian Bildungsroman ?
options: Ruth Pawar Jhabvala, Heat and Dust
Jeanette Winterson, Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit
items.explanation: Jeanette Winterson's semi-autobiographical debut novel Oranges Are Not the Only Fruit (1985) is a classic lesbian Bildungsroman. It follows Jeanette, an adopted girl raised in a strict English Pentecostal community, as she discovers her lesbian identity and comes of age.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q23
items.stem:
Which among the following are written by Mikhail Bakhtin?
A. White Mythology
B. Freudianism: A Marxist Critique
C. The Ideology of the Aesthetics
D. Rabelais and His World
E. Morphology of the Folktale
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Rabelais and His World (1965, D) and the Bakhtin Circle treatise Freudianism: A Marxist Critique (1927, B, published under V. N. Voloshinov's name and widely attributed to Bakhtin) are associated with Mikhail Bakhtin. White Mythology is by Jacques Derrida, The Ideology of the Aesthetic is by Terry Eagleton, and Morphology of the Folktale is by Vladimir Propp.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q24
items.stem:
John Heywood wrote a farcical interlude called The Four P's.
Who were the Four P's ?
options: Palmer, a Pardoner, a Pothecary, a Pedlar
Printer, a Pedlar, a Pothecary, a Palmer
Pedlar, a Parson, a Palmer, a Pothecary
Palmer, a Pedlar, a Pothecary, a Packer
items.explanation: Tudor dramatist John Heywood's comic verse interlude The Playe Called the Foure PP (c. 1530, printed c. 1544) features a lying contest among four characters whose professions begin with P: a Palmer, a Pardoner, a 'Pothecary (Apothecary), and a Pedlar.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q25
items.stem:
Arrange the following texts in chronological order of their year of publication:
A. Coolie
B. The Big Heart
C. The Village
D. Two Leaves and a Bud
E. Seven Summers
items.explanation: The publication years of Mulk Raj Anand's novels in chronological order are: Coolie (1936), Two Leaves and a Bud (1937), The Village (1939), The Big Heart (1945), and Seven Summers (1951). This corresponds to A -> D -> C -> B -> E.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q26
items.stem:
In which of his voyages, Gulliver
discovered mountain-like beings ?
items.explanation: In Part II of Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726), Lemuel Gulliver voyages to the land of Brobdingnag, whose inhabitants are giant, mountain-like beings standing roughly sixty feet tall.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q27
items.stem:
Given below are two statements
Statement I: In Waiting for Godot, it is Vladimir who questions the Boy who comes from Godot towards the end of the two
Acts.
Statement II: In Waiting for Godot, it is Estragon who says, "Nothing happens, nobody comes, nobody goes, it's awful."
In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
items.explanation: In Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot (1953), Vladimir interrogates Godot's messenger Boy at the end of both acts (Statement I is true), and Estragon speaks the famous line 'Nothing happens, nobody comes, nobody goes, it's awful!' in Act I (Statement II is true).

items.title: Mock #11 · Q28
items.stem:
Who/Which among the following gave the expression, "a leopard can't change its spots," to
English language ?
items.explanation: The proverb 'a leopard cannot change its spots' entered the English language from the King James Bible (1611), specifically the Book of Jeremiah 13:23: 'Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?'

items.title: Mock #11 · Q29
items.stem:
Who are the co-editors of Chutneyfying English: The Phenomenon of Hinglish?
(a) Jamuna Kachru
(b) Rita Kothari
(c) Rupert Snell
(d) Alastair Pennycook
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Chutneyfying English: The Phenomenon of Hinglish (2011), an influential collection of essays examining the hybrid mixing of Hindi and English in Indian popular culture, media, and advertising, was co-edited by Rita Kothari (b) and Rupert Snell (c).

items.title: Mock #11 · Q30
items.stem: Which of the following works is set in the backdrop of the religious persecution in Mexico?
items.explanation: Graham Greene's novel The Power and the Glory (1940) is set in the Mexican state of Tabasco during the 1930s anti-clerical Calles regime, following a fugitive 'whisky priest' hunted by a socialist lieutenant.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q31
items.stem:
Listed below are the titles of novels and the sources to which they are aligned by readers. Match them appropriately :
List – I
(I) Peter Carey's Jack Maggs
(II) J.M. Coetzee's Foe
(III) Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea
(IV) William Golding's Lord of the Flies

List – II
(1) Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe
(2) Charlotte Bronte's Jane Eyre
(3) R.M. Ballantyne's The Coral Island
(4) Charles Dickens's Great Expectations

Codes : (I) (II) (III) (IV)
items.explanation: Peter Carey's Jack Maggs rewrites Dickens's Great Expectations (4), J.M. Coetzee's Foe rewrites Defoe's Robinson Crusoe (1), Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea is a postcolonial prequel to Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre (2), and William Golding's Lord of the Flies subverts R.M. Ballantyne's The Coral Island (3).

items.title: Mock #11 · Q32
items.stem:
Chapter III of Oliver Twist opens ith a narratorial remark about Oliver being punished for
“the commission of the impious and profane offence of asking for ore.” What did Oliver
ask for ore ?
items.explanation: In Chapter II-III of Charles Dickens's Oliver Twist (1838), the famished workhouse boys cast lots and Oliver famously approaches the master with his basin and spoon, uttering 'Please, sir, I want some more' gruel to eat, which the workhouse board treats as an impious outrage.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q33
items.stem:
Ear-training in ELT is easily achieved by :

(a)
composition

(b)
dictation

(c)
cloze tests

(d)
listening exercises

(e)
précis writing
items.explanation: In English Language Teaching (ELT), ear-training—the development of auditory discrimination of sounds, stress, and intonation—is directly achieved through oral-aural tasks such as dictation (b) and listening exercises (d), whereas composition, cloze tests, and précis writing test reading and writing skills.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q34
items.stem: W.B. Yeats's "Easter 1916" is
options: a response to a major political uprising
a reminiscence of his visit to a nursery school
a love poem for Maud Gonne
an ode to his native country
items.explanation: W. B. Yeats's poem 'Easter, 1916' is a profound elegiac meditation on the Easter Rising of April 1916 in Dublin, in which Irish Republicans staged an armed insurrection against British rule, declaring that 'A terrible beauty is born.'

items.title: Mock #11 · Q35
items.stem:
Arrange the following works of criticism in chronological order:
A. T. S. Eliot, The Use of Poetry and the Use of Criticism
B. J.C. Smith, A Study of Wordsworth
C. D. G. James, Scepticism and Poetry
D. Marjorie L. Barstow, Wordsworth's Theory of Poetic Diction
E. Josephine Miles, Pathetic Fallacy in the Nineteenth Century
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Barstow (1917), Eliot (1933), D. G. James (1937), Josephine Miles (1942) and J. C. Smith (1944). So the order is D, A, C, E, B.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q36
items.stem:
In Spenser's Re Faerie Queene there
are
the
allegorized
moral
and
religious
virtues
with
their
counterparts in the vices. Identify the
correctly matched set
options: Una - Truth Guyon - Temperance Duessa - Deceit Orgoglio - Pride
Una - Pride Guyon - Deceit Duessa - Temperance Orgoglio - Truth
Una - Deceit Guyon - Pride Duessa - Temperance Orgoglio - Truth
Una - Temperance Guyon - Truth Duessa - Pride Orgoglio - Deceit
items.explanation: In Edmund Spenser's allegorical epic The Faerie Queene (1590–1596), Una personifies Truth and the true Church (Book I), Sir Guyon represents the virtue of Temperance (Book II), Duessa embodies falsehood and deceit, and the giant Orgoglio symbolizes spiritual and worldly pride.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q37
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Linguists, being primarily interested in the scientific study of language, approach language dispassionately.
Statement II: Linguists are necessarily polyglots who bring their own biases to language study.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
items.explanation: Modern linguistics is the objective, descriptive, and scientific study of human language (Statement I is correct), and linguists need not be polyglots nor inject personal prescriptive biases into linguistic analysis (Statement II is incorrect).

items.title: Mock #11 · Q38
items.stem: The poetry of Wordsworth and Coleridge was notably influenced by...
items.explanation: The early romantic poetry and radical democratic ideals of William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge were profoundly shaped by the political, intellectual, and social ferment of the French Revolution (1789).

items.title: Mock #11 · Q39
items.stem:
Which of the following definitions are wrong?

A Africative sound involves the close approximation of two articulators

B. Stops involve closure of the articulators to obstruct the air-stream

C. Raising of the front of the tongue to form a secondary articulation is called velarisation

D.ATrill occurs when an articulator is held loosely fairly close to another articulator so that it sets into vibration

E. Raising of the back of the tongue while making another articulation elsewhere is called palatalisation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Statements C and E provide inverted linguistic definitions: palatalisation involves raising the front of the tongue towards the hard palate (not velarisation), whereas velarisation involves raising the back of the tongue towards the soft palate or velum (not palatalisation).

items.title: Mock #11 · Q40
items.stem:
To refer to the unresolvable difficulties
a text may open up, Derrida makes use
of the term
items.explanation: Adopted from Greek philosophy (meaning an 'unpassable path'), aporia is used by Jacques Derrida in deconstruction to denote a point of undecidability or an unresolvable logical impasse where a text contradicts and undermines its own rhetorical premises.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q41
items.stem: Match List - I with List - II. List - I (Character) List - II (Work) (A) Christophine (I) Wuthering Heights (B) Zillah (II) Wide Sargasso Sea (C) Estella (III) Things Fall Apart (D) Ekwefi (IV) Great Expectations Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The correct character-to-work matches are: Christophine is the loyal Martinican nurse in Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) [(A)-(II)]; Zillah is the servant at Wuthering Heights in Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights (1847) [(B)-(I)]; Estella is Miss Havisham's haughty adopted daughter in Charles Dickens's Great Expectations (1861) [(C)-(IV)]; and Ekwefi is Okonkwo's second wife in Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart (1958) [(D)-(III)].

items.title: Mock #11 · Q42
items.stem:
F. R. Leavis and Q. D. Leavis launched a critical journal devoted to the moral centrality of
English Studies.  Name the Journal.
items.explanation: F. R. Leavis and Q. D. Leavis founded and edited the highly influential critical quarterly Scrutiny at Cambridge from 1932 to 1953, championing the supreme moral seriousness and cultural necessity of literary analysis.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q43
items.stem:
Which of the following can be classified as Science Fiction ?
(A) The Moonlight
(B) Time Machine
(C) Great Expectations
(D) The Golden Gate
(E) Brave New World
items.explanation: H. G. Wells's The Time Machine (1895) and Aldous Huxley's Brave New World (1932) are landmark works of science fiction dealing with time travel and totalitarian future biotechnology. Great Expectations is Victorian realist fiction, and The Golden Gate is a verse novel.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q44
items.stem: Who is the only one of Milton's contemporaries to be mentioned by name in Paradise Lost ?
items.explanation: Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), whom John Milton visited near Florence in 1638, is the only contemporary of Milton mentioned in Paradise Lost (referred to as 'the Tuscan artist' in Book I, line 288, and by name as 'Galileo' in Book V, line 262).

items.title: Mock #11 · Q45
items.stem: Indicate the correct chronological order of publication of the following literary works: (A) Beowulf (B) Divina Commedia (C) Summa Theologica (D) Le Morte d' Arthur (E) Canterbury Tales Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The chronological order of composition and publication is: the Old English epic Beowulf (c. 8th-10th century), Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae (c. 1265-1274), Dante's Divina Commedia (c. 1308-1320), Geoffrey Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales (c. 1387-1400), and Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur (1485) [(A), (C), (B), (E), (D)].

items.title: Mock #11 · Q46
items.stem:
Among Derek Walcott's plays, which one is an exploration of colonial relationships through
the Robinson Crusoe story ?
items.explanation: Derek Walcott's two-character play Pantomime (1978), set in Tobago, explores postcolonial master-servant power dynamics as white English hotel owner Harry Trewe and his Black Trinidadian handyman Jackson Phillip rehearse a role-reversed musical version of Robinson Crusoe.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q47
items.stem:
Here are sentences labelled Assertion (A) and Reason (R) :
Assertion (A) : In Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf ? George and Martha's blue and green-eyed son is a myth.
Reason (R) : He is a creation of the couple's imagination originating from their sense of sterility and vacuum in life.
In the light of (A) and (R), which of the following is correct ?
options: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: In Edward Albee's Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (1962), George and Martha's twenty-one-year-old son is an imaginary construct ('myth') invented by the childless couple to cope with their infertility and emotional emptiness, making both (A) and (R) true with (R) as the correct explanation.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q48
items.stem:
Which of the following novels is NOT
a Partition novel ?
items.explanation: Shashi Deshpande's Sahitya Akademi Award-winning novel That Long Silence (1988) is a feminist domestic novel about a Mumbai housewife named Jaya re-evaluating her marriage, whereas Chaman Nahal's Azadi (1975), Bhisham Sahni's Tamas (1973), and Anita Desai's Clear Light of Day (1980) are all Partition novels.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q49
items.stem:
Which among the following are not the slave narratives?

A. Black Boy by Richard Wright

B. An Untamed State by Roxane Gay

C. Behind the Scenes by Elizabeth Keckley

D. The Nature of Blood by Caryl Phillips

E. Up From Slavery by Booker T. Washington

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Roxane Gay's An Untamed State (2014) is a contemporary novel about a kidnapping in Haiti, and Caryl Phillips's The Nature of Blood (1997) is a historical novel addressing Othello and the Holocaust, so neither work is a slave narrative. In contrast, Elizabeth Keckley's Behind the Scenes (1868) and Booker T. Washington's Up From Slavery (1901) are canonical African American slave narratives.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q62
items.stem: Which of the following statements holds true in regard to "Sentimental Comedy"?
options: It is a dramatic composition which satirises the manners and affectations of a class.
It is a dramatic composition that focuses on characters, each of them representing a type personality.
It is a dramatic composition that depicts how seriously young people take love, and how foolishly it makes them behave.

It is a species of dramatic composition in which the virtues of private life are exhibited, rather than the vices exposed; and the distresses rather than the faults of mankind make our interest in the piece.
items.explanation: Option 4 quotes Oliver Goldsmith's classic definition of Sentimental Comedy from 'An Essay on the Theatre; or, A Comparison Between Laughing and Sentimental Comedy' (1773): a genre that exhibits middle-class private virtues and pathetic distresses to evoke sympathetic tears rather than satirizing vices.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q63
items.stem: Choose the correct option(s) in the New Historicist reading of Dalit writing: (A) Dalit writing does not essentialise Indian society, culture and identity. (B) Dalit writing has inflected the immanent metanarratives. (C) There is no single location of Dalit writing. (D) Dalit writing is only a political category. (E) Dalit writing is not grounded in history. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: A New Historicist reading highlights that Dalit literature refuses to essentialize Indian society as a uniform monolith (A), disrupts dominant upper-caste nationalist metanarratives (B), and originates from diverse, plurivocal regional and linguistic locations across India (C). Statements (D) and (E) are false because Dalit writing is rooted in deep material history and represents an ontological aesthetic rather than a narrow political label.

items.explanation: In research methodology, a hypothesis is a tentative, provisional explanation of a phenomenon (B) or a testable proposition assumed to be true for the sake of investigation and argument (D). items.explanation: The correct chronological order of publication is: John Milton's Paradise Lost (1667), Alexander Pope's The Dunciad (1728), Percy Bysshe Shelley's Alastor, or The Spirit of Solitude (1816), and John Keats's Lamia (1820).

items.stem:

items.explanation: Sir William Jones delivered this famous address on February 2, 1786, during his Third Anniversary Discourse to the Asiatic Society of Bengal in Calcutta. His observation that Sanskrit shares an intricate grammatical and structural affinity with Greek and Latin founded modern comparative philology and established the Indo-European language family.

items.title: Mock #11 · Q96
items.meta: Unit IV / Unit VIII: Prose & Criticism
items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:
Poetry in its use of language continually distorts and denies the structure of reality to exalt the structure of the self. By means of rhyme, assonance or alliteration it couples together words which have no rational connection, that is, no nexus through the world of external reality. It breaks the word up into lines of arbitrary length, cutting across their logical construction. It breaks down their associations, derived from the world of external reality, by means of inversion and every variety of artificial stressing and counterpoint. Thus the world of external reality recedes and the world of instinct, the affective emotional linkage behind the words, becomes the world of reality... In the novel, too, the subjective elements are valued for themselves, and rise to view, but in a different way. The novel blots out external reality by substituting a more or less consistent mock reality which has sufficient 'stuff' to stand between the reader and reality. This means that in the novel the emotional associations attach not to words but to the moving current of mock reality symbolised by the words. This is why rhythm, 'preciousness', and style are alien to the novel; why the novel translates so well; why novels are not composed of words. They are composed of scenes, actions, stuff, people, just as plays are.

In the above passage, Christopher Caudwell's statement, "Poetry in its use of language continually distorts and denies the structure of reality to exalt the structure of the self" implies:
options: The pragmatic function of poetry that reflects the social reality through expressive language
Poetry exalts the "structure of the self" by privileging the notion of the 'egotistical sublime'
The capacity of poetry to draw attention to itself as an aesthetic object or artefact
The mimetic function of poetry that alludes to the world of external reality in simple, clear language
items.explanation: In this passage from Illusion and Reality (1937), Christopher Caudwell's claim that poetry distorts external reality to 'exalt the structure of the self' implies that poetry privileges subjective, instinctive, ego-centered emotional experience ('the egotistical sublime') over objective external reality.

Poetry in its use of language continually distorts and denies the structure of reality to exalt the structure of the self. By means of rhyme, assonance or alliteration it couples together words which have no rational connection, that is, no nexus through the world of external reality. It breaks the word up into lines of arbitrary length, cutting across their logical construction. It breaks down their associations, derived from the world of external reality, by means of inversion and every variety of artificial stressing and counterpoint. Thus the world of external reality recedes and the world of instinct, the affective emotional linkage behind the words, becomes the world of reality... In the novel, too, the subjective elements are valued for themselves, and rise to view, but in a different way. The novel blots out external reality by substituting a more or less consistent mock reality which has sufficient 'stuff' to stand between the reader and reality. This means that in the novel the emotional associations attach not to words but to the moving current of mock reality symbolised by the words. This is why rhythm, 'preciousness', and style are alien to the novel; why the novel translates so well; why novels are not composed of words. They are composed of scenes, actions, stuff, people, just as plays are.

What does the word "assonance" mean?
options: repetition of identical or similar consonants
repetition of identical or similar clauses
repetition of identical or similar phrases
repetition of identical or similar vowels
items.explanation: Assonance is a prosodic and figurative device consisting of the repetition of identical or similar vowel sounds—especially in stressed syllables—in nearby words whose consonant sounds differ.
